To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the NSF should allocate more funds to nanobiotechnology research than it currently does, and it should do this by allocating funds across time, rather than across universities, because of network effects.

1) the optimal allocation of research funds to universities is a function of their own past knowledge output and the knowledge output of other universities in previous years, 2) the optimal amount spent on nanobiotechnology research in any given year is a function of the knowledge outputs of all universities in previous years and the amount spent by the NSF in previous years, and 3) the optimal amount of research funding spent on nanobiotech research is increasing over time.

(i) The NSF should allocate funds to universities based on the universities’ current stock of knowledge and their current spending on R&D, but not based on past knowledge production; (ii) The NSF should also allocate funds based on the universities current stock of knowledge produced in other universities; and (iii) The NSF should not allocate funds based on past spending on R&D.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the optimal allocation of research funds across universities and across time to maximize the aggregate output of knowledge in a particular field of science.
the following questions: How do the knowledge outputs produced by universities depend on the stock of knowledge of the university itself and the stocks of knowledge at other universities?
the optimal allocation of funds for nanobiotech research by a funding agency such as the National Science Foundation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the model is not a good fit to the data.

the NSF should spend 0.8 percent more on nanobiotechnology R&D in 2005 than it actually did, and that this additional spending would increase the total output of nanobiotechnology Ph.D.s by 2.4 percent, research publications by 2.5 percent, and patents by 1.8 percent.
the optimal allocation of NSF funds for nanobiotechnological research would increase the aggregate amounts of Ph.D. degrees and publications, and decrease the aggregate amounts of patents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NSF could have increased the total output of Ph.D.s, publications, and patents produced by US universities in the nanobiotechnology research area by 10–15 % by optimally allocating its funds.
the NSF should spend more funds in 1990 and 2005 than it actually did.

a policy maker who wants to optimize the production of nanobiotechnology knowledge should focus on increasing funding to universities with the largest knowledge stocks and the highest marginal productivity of funds, and on increasing funding to the most productive fields within universities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the optimal time path of the research funds is not constant over time.
the optimal allocation of funds is very different from the actual allocations.

the NSF should invest heavily in nanobiotechnology research in universities that have already invested heavily in the life sciences and engineering, and that are currently investing heavily in nanobiotech research.
